translations.title: To a Lady Who Asked Him for Something of His Own
translations.text:
The music is neither sweet nor good,
though well sung, my lady,
if it strays from the tune of the words;
instead it brings displeasure, vexation, and pain.

But if the music happens to sound
in keeping with what is sung,
instead of the grief it breeds in the soul,
it leaves her filled with sweet imaginings.

You, who can move mountains
to the sound of song, do not sing of anger,
nor of the secret sorrow that consumes me.

Let my tears remain mine alone;
sing instead of the beauty of your eyes:
the song will then accord with what is sung.

translations.title: To the Count of Feria
translations.text:
While fierce French fury shows itself
united with the trembling barbarian,
while the dreadful Protestant alliance
plans to unsettle our faith and homeland,

Mars arms your right hand, my lord,
upon which Victory waits,
following that trace of valor
which virtue guides toward immortality.

Already I seem to see your glory’s
high radiance shining so brightly
that it will dazzle your father’s might.

My only fear is that so great a tale
will not be set in everlasting song
unless you yourself become your own chronicler.

translations.title: Go, False Vision, Do Not Torment Me
translations.text:
Go, false vision, do not torment me;
leave me be, I do not wish to believe you.
My fortune lies in not finding out;
you would have me know, and everyone else too.

Go, cowardly fear, and tell me nothing
that does not accord with my faith;
go, mad suspicion; this is my fate:
to be slain by a thousand seeming shadows.

Go, hellish fire, jealous fury,
fierce imagination, cruel and harmful;
do not disabuse me when I ask you not to.

Believing in happiness wrongs no one.
Why would you make my lady seem so suspect,
and inflict this strange evil on me?

translations.title: To a Lady Weeping for Her Dead Servant
translations.text:
The nymph Flora wept for shepherd Menalcas,
for the strange and grievous, cruel event;
and from her lovely face—alas, hard fate!—
the roses darkened and lost their color.

Now she makes herself weep, then turns and weeps,
turning her tears to great pearls;
now she lies dead and cold, and if death
lets her breathe, she sometimes says:

“Fate, if you fell in love with my beloved,
cut the uncertain thread of my life;
you shall enjoy your power, I my deception.

But, ah, what am I saying? You did not miss:
in killing him, you killed me too;
you struck him, yet I feel the wound.”

translations.title: I Would Speak of You So Highly
translations.text:
I would speak of you so highly
that the world might see what I see in you,
if speech could match desire.

Even if I searched the fairest heavens,
among all precious, lovely things on earth,
I find none that resembles you by a hair;
no one is to blame for not daring to compare.

White things, crystal, gold, and roses,
rubies, pearls, and snow,
compared with your face,
are painted things beside the living.

Before you the stars,
as before the sun, are less beautiful.
The sun is more radiant,
but to my eyes not so lovely.
What can I say, when all I see
is ugly beside you?

Change your name, then, my lady:
call yourself Beauty, Beauty Maria.

translations.title: Alas, What Fierce Conflict
translations.text:
Alas, what fierce conflict,
my lady, between the soul and senses,
when I would have you pity my groans!

None dares speak;
each grows timid and excuses itself
to the yearning soul,
which blames the tongue for its confusion.

Confused, it says it will tell you
of my pain, if fear of some misstep
would only leave it be;
but a cold dread wears the heart away,
and, stunned, when it would tell you something,
it says nothing.

The heart dislikes this excuse
and says the fault lies with the tongue,
for complaint is the tongue’s work.
Each diminishes the other;
empty thought cannot advise
a mind distraught.

I feel reason, once their mistress,
now their servant,
and courage weakens hour by hour.
My hand no longer uses
the means it once did;
fear makes it timid and turns it aside.

The blood runs cold
to the weakest part, and in confusion
the sad body trembles, sweating ice.
O furious care!
If the soul struggles against the senses,
who will tell you to pity my groans?

translations.title: Nobles and Servants
translations.text:
Those nobles of old celebrated in tales,
formidable champions
with imposing faces,
whose bodies, built of giant bones,
seemed rooted in the earth.

Were they to return, wishing to see
the heirs of their immortal name,
they would find base-born upstarts
frequenting ministers’ palaces,
a degraded, grasping breed;

weaklings in sashes, breastplates, and padding.
Only then could those nobles understand
that in recent times their daughters
have mixed much servants’ blood
with their noble lineage.

translations.title: To J.-Y. Colonna
translations.text:
Nobles and Servants\n\nThose nobles of old celebrated in tales,
formidable champions
with imposing faces,
whose bodies, built of giant bones,
seemed rooted in the earth.

Were they to return, wishing to see
the heirs of their immortal name,
they would find base-born upstarts
frequenting ministers’ palaces,
a degraded, grasping breed;

weaklings in sashes, breastplates, and padding.
Only then could those nobles understand
that in recent times their daughters
have mixed much servants’ blood
with their noble lineage.

translations.title: To Madame Aguado
translations.text:
Sapphire column, embroidered with arabesques,
appear again! The nest’s rowers take flight;
from your brow crowned with blue to your granite feet,
the purple of Judea unfolds.

If you see Benares leaning on its river,
loose your torso with your burnished golden bow,
for I am the vulture flying over Patani,
and the sea is flooded with white butterflies.

Lanasá! Let your veil float on the waters!
Give purple flowers to the stream.
The snow of Cathay is falling on the Atlantic.

Meanwhile the red-faced priestess still sleeps
beneath the arch of the sun,
and nothing has disturbed the stern portal.

translations.title: To Madame Ida Dumas
To Luisa D’Or, Queen
translations.text:
The trembling patriarch shook the universe.
Isis, the Mother, at last rose from her bed,
gave her savage husband a look of hatred,
and the old ardor blazed in her green eyes.

“Look at him,” she says, “that wicked old man sleeps;
all the world’s ice has passed through his mouth.
Beware his foot; put out his crooked eye:
he is king of volcanoes, god of winters.”

“The eagle has passed: Napoleon calls me;
for him I have donned Cybele’s mantle.
I am Hermes’ wife, Osiris’ sister…”

The goddess had escaped in her golden shell;
the sea returned her worshiped image to us,
and the skies shone beneath Iris’ scarf.

translations.title: To Madame Sand
translations.text:
“That rock hollowed by art, a masterpiece
from another age, that rock of Tarascon
once sheltered giants come down from the heights,
whose bones bear sure witness.”

Lord Du Bartas, I am of your lineage,
I join my verse to your verse of old;
but the cold descendants of the Counts of Foix
need witnesses to speak today.

I passed through Salzburg beneath trembling cliffs;
there Austria’s stork feeds the kites.
Barbarossa and Richard honored that refuge.

Snow reigns on the heights of its untouched peaks,
and they have told me these are the white bones
of ancient mountains gnawed by the Flood.

translations.title: He Was That Madman, Sublime Fool
translations.text:
He was that madman, sublime fool…
that forgotten Icarus climbing the skies,
that lost Phaethon beneath the divine bolt,
the fair wounded Attis whom Cybele revives!

The augur examined the victim’s side,
the earth grew drunk on that precious blood…
The dazed cosmos hung upon its axes,
and Olympus wavered for an instant toward the abyss.

“Tell me!” Caesar cried to Jupiter Ammon,
who is this new god who has mastered the earth?
And if no god, is he at least a demon…?

But the summoned oracle fell forever silent;
only one in the world could explain the mystery:
he who gave his soul to the children of clay.

translations.title: Fantasy
translations.text:
There is a tune for which I would give
all Mozart, Rossini, and all of Weber,
an old, languishing, mournful tune
that brings its secret charms to me alone.

Each time I hear it, my soul grows
two hundred years younger—it is set in Louis XIII’s time—
and I seem to see a green hillside
turning gold in the sunset,

then a castle of brick and stone,
with windows tinted red,
ringed by broad parks, with a stream at its feet
running among the flowers;

then a lady at her lofty window,
fair-haired, dark-eyed, dressed in old-fashioned clothes,
whom perhaps I saw in another life,
and whom I remember.

translations.title: The Disinherited
translations.text:
I am the Shadowy One, the widower, the unconsoled,
Prince of Aquitaine, whose tower is gone;
my only star has died, and my starry lute
bears within it Melancholy’s black sun.

In the night tomb, you who comforted me,
restore Pausilippo and the Italian sea,
that flower so dear to my desolate soul,
and the vine where tendril twines with rose.

Am I Amor or Phoebus? Lusignan or Byron?
My brow still reddens from the Queen’s kiss;
I dreamed in the Grotto where the Siren swims…

Twice victorious, I have crossed Acheron,
sometimes playing on Orpheus’ lyre
the Saint’s sighs, at others the Fairy’s cries.

translations.title: Anteros
translations.text:
“Why is there such rage in my heart,” you ask,
and such a defiant head on my supple neck?
Because I come from the race of Antaeus
and turn the victor god’s arrows back.

I am one of those the Avenger inspires;
he marked my brow with his angry mouth.
Beneath Abel’s pallor, stained with blood,
I sometimes bear Cain’s relentless blush!

Jehovah, he who, conquered by your genius,
last of all cried from hell’s depths, “O tyranny!”
is my grandfather Belus, or my father Dagon…

Three times I was bathed in Cocytus’ waters;
sole protector of my Amalekite mother,
I sow the old dragon’s teeth at her feet.

translations.title: To J.-Y. Colonna
translations.text:
Do you know, Daphne, that old romance
beneath the sycamore… under white mulberries,
beneath the weeping olive or trembling willows,
that love song forever beginning anew?

Do you recognize the temple’s vast peristyle,
the bitter lemons whose rind you bit,
and the fatal cave of unwary guests
where the defeated serpent’s seed sleeps?

Do you know why the volcano has opened again?
One day we touched it with our nimble feet,
covering the far horizon with its dust!

Since a ship broke our clay gods,
beneath the palm of Virgil’s urn,
pale hydrangeas mingle with green laurel.

translations.title: Artemis
translations.text:
The thirteenth returns… becomes the first again;
and the only one is always, or the only moment.
So who are you, queen—the first or the last?
And you, king—the sole lover or the final one?

To love the one I loved from cradle to coffin;
the one I loved alone still loves me tenderly!
Is it death, or the dead woman… O delight, O torment!
The rose she holds is no rose, but a hollyhock.

Neapolitan saint with hands of fire,
rose with a violet soul, flower of Saint Gudula:
have you found your cross in the desert skies?

Fall, white roses, for you insult my gods;
fall, white phantoms from your burning heaven:
the saint of the abyss is holier in my eyes.

translations.title: To Pan
translations.text:
Seated in a forest glen,
by a reed-fringed stream,
I mused one day, then, growing drowsy,
found myself sunk in a dream.

A figure rose from the brook,
half man and half goat;
he had hooves instead of feet,
and a beard adorned his throat.

On a rustic reed pipe
that hybrid creature played sweetly,
and I forgot all earthly care,
for I knew that it was Pan.

Nymphs and satyrs gathered
to enjoy the merry sound.

Too soon I woke, regretful,
and returned to human dwellings;
but I would live in country valleys
and hear Pan’s pipe again.

translations.title: Mirage
translations.text:
I do not know if that world ever existed,
draining away on time’s waters.
Often I have seen it in purple mist,
flickering in the abyss of some vague dream:
its strange towers, unusual rivers,
giant labyrinths, luminous caverns,
and tangled skies, like those that tremble,
anxious at night’s infernal omen.

Its marshes reach a desolate shore
where immense birds writhe;
and on a windy height
an ancient people raise white bell towers
whose evening chimes I still hear.

I know not what land it is… I dare not ask
when, or why, I went or shall go there.

translations.title: The Yule Horror
translations.text:
Snow lies in the fields,
and the valleys are frozen;
deep midnight
hangs darkly over the world.
Yet a glimpse of light on the peaks
reveals profane feasts of old.

Death is in the clouds,
fear is in the night,
for the dead in their shrouds
celebrate the setting sun,
singing wild songs in the woods as they dance
around Yule’s moldy white altar.

A wind from beyond this world
moves through the oak forest,
whose morbid branches drown
in a tangle of delirious mistletoe,
for these are the powers of darkness that endure
in the tombs of the lost race of Druids.

translations.title: Oceanus
translations.text:
Sometimes I pause upon the shore
where sorrows pour their streams,
and turbulent waters sigh and moan
of secrets they dare not tell.
From deep chasms in nameless valleys,
from hills and plains no mortal knows,
the mystic tide and sullen surf
suggest, like cursed sorcerers,
a thousand terrors swollen with fear
that ages long forgotten once beheld.

O salt winds that sadly sweep
the naked regions of the deep;
o pale wild waves, remembering
the chaos Earth has left behind;
one thing alone I ask of you:
keep your ancient knowledge hidden forever!

translations.title: Where Poe Once Walked
translations.text:
Shadows wander eternally in this land,
dreaming of centuries gone forever;
great elms rise solemnly among tombstones and mounds,
their high canopy spread over a hidden world of another time.
A light of memory illumines the whole scene,
dead leaves whisper of vanished days,
longing for sights and sounds that will never return.

Sad and solitary, a specter glides along
the paths his living footsteps once took;
not everyone can see him, though his song
resounds through time with strange fascination.
Only the few who know the secret of his magic
can find Poe’s shadow among these graves.

translations.title: Hesperia
translations.text:
The winter sunset, glowing behind the spires
and half-detached chimneys of this shadowy sphere,
opens wide doors to some forgotten year
of ancient splendors and divine desires.
Future wonders burn in those fires,
full of adventure and untouched by fear;
a row of sphinxes marks the way
between trembling walls and towers toward distant lyres.

It is the land where beauty’s sense flowers,
where every unexplained memory has its root,
where Time’s great river begins its downward course
through the vast abyss in dreams of starlit hours.
Dreams draw us near… but ancient knowledge repeats
that no human foot has ever trod its secrets.

translations.title: The Book
translations.text:
The place was dark and dusty, a lost corner
in a maze of old lanes beside the docks,
smelling of strange things from overseas,
amid curious scraps of fog scattered by the west wind.
Smoke- and frost-clouded diamond panes
barely revealed heaps of books, like twisted trees
rotting from floor to ceiling… traces
of ancient knowledge crumbling at bargain prices.

I entered, spellbound, and from a cobwebbed heap
picked up the nearest volume and read at random,
trembling at strange words that seemed to conceal
some monstrous secret for whoever found it.
Then, searching for an old, sly bookseller,
I found only the echo of a laugh.

translations.title: My Soul Is Like the Sea
translations.text:
My soul is like the sea:
it has waves and storms;
but in its depths
many pearls are to be found.

translations.title: My Soul Is Like the Sea
translations.text:
My soul is like the sea:
    it has waves and storms;
    but in its depths
    many pearls are to be found.\n\nVersion by Guillermo Matta

translations.title: Put Your Hand Upon My Breast, Girl
translations.text:
Put your hand upon my breast, girl.
Do you not feel a gloomy unrest within?
It is that in my soul there lives a craftsman
who keeps driving nails into my coffin.

He works without rest all day,
and through the night he works on.
Finish soon, master, my soul longs for it;
let me rest in peace.

translations.title: Beat the Drum Without Fear
translations.text:
Beat the drum without fear,
and embrace the canteen girl:
there is the whole science of it,
the truest meaning
of the finest book.

Let your drum’s noise
wake the sleeping world;
play reveille with ardor.
March on, ever upright!
That is sovereign wisdom.

Hegel’s profoundest,
most complete meaning—
I learned it, and it is proven:
I am a worldly lad,
and a skilled drummer.

translations.title: Fortune
translations.text:
Ah, Lady Fortune! In vain
you show yourself disdainful. Your favors
I shall win with courageous spirit,
like all brave fighters.

In the fierce contest you will fall subdued;
I forge the yoke to which you’ll be harnessed.
But seeing you disarmed at my feet,
I feel a mortal wound within my heart.

Red blood wells up in a river,
and the sweet breath of life…
when at last the triumph I desired is mine,
I feel my strength give way, and I am dying.

translations.title: Ah, Lady Fortune, In Vain
translations.text:
Ah, Lady Fortune! In vain
you show yourself disdainful. Your favors
I shall win with courageous spirit,
like all brave fighters.

In the fierce contest you will fall subdued;
I forge the yoke to which you’ll be harnessed.
But seeing you disarmed at my feet,
I feel a mortal wound within my heart.

Red blood wells up in a river,
and the sweet breath of life…
when at last the triumph I desired is mine,
I feel my strength give way, and I am dying.

translations.title: The Butterfly in Love
translations.text:
In love, the butterfly
flies from the cool rose
over its fragrant cup;
a ray of burning sun
bathes it lovingly
in golden light.

But whom does the rose love?
Who deserves the fair one’s love,
I would like to know?
Is it the nightingale who sings,
or the star that rises
as evening wanes?

I know not whom the rose adores;
but my breast holds tender love
for all: fair rose,
ray of sun, bright star,
butterfly and nightingale.

translations.title: Once I Dreamed of Ardor
translations.text:
Once I dreamed of ardent love,
of lovely curls, myrtle and mignonette,
sweet lips and bitter words,
sad melodies of sorrowful songs.

Long since my dream lies scattered, lifeless;
my dearest dream is scattered now.
Only what I once poured
with untamed ardor into tender rhymes remains.

Do you remain, orphaned song?
Fade away too, and seek the dream I lost long ago;
if you find it, greet it for me.
I send a fleeting breath to a fleeting shadow.

translations.title: The Wounded Knight
translations.text:
Many tales I have heard;
none so cruel as this:
a well-born gentleman
lies grievously wounded by love,
and his lady is unfaithful.

For her treachery and betrayal,
he, foolishly adoring her,
should scorn her;
he should regard his pain
as an infamous weakness.

He would challenge her in the lists,
crying out:
“I love a lovely maiden;
whoever finds fault with her,
come forth and cross swords with me.”

Perhaps all would fall silent;
but not his distress.
At last their weapons would have to wound,
if they wished to fight,
his wretched heart.

translations.title: They Loved with Frenzied Passion
translations.text:
They loved with frenzied passion:
she was a prostitute; he was a thief.
When he plotted some crime,
she lay on the bed and laughed.

He idled all day without a care,
and spent the night in his lover’s arms.
When the police took him away,
she watched from the balcony and laughed.

From prison he sent word to her
that he could not live without her love.
She shook her nosy head from side to side
and laughed.

At six they hanged him; at seven
his body was taken to burial.
By eight that same day
she was drunk, and laughing.

translations.title: Every Afternoon in the Garden
translations.text:
Every afternoon in the garden,
as evening is about to fall,
the sultan’s lovely daughter
descends to stroll there.

Beside the ringing fountain
she sometimes pauses,
watching the clear jets leap
and hearing them fall.

Every afternoon, as evening falls,
the handsome slave comes too,
and calmly he is seen
beside the fountain, listening
to the jets as well.

Each afternoon his face grows paler.
One day the princess hurries up to him:
“What is your name? What is your homeland, slave?”
“Arabia gave me birth;
they called me Mohammed.
I am of those Azraites
who die when they truly love.”

translations.title: Spring Festival
translations.text:
How sad, O Spring,
how sad your joys are today!
Grieving maidens hurry
in an anxious throng,
tunics loosened,
hair disordered,
with mournful cries calling,
“Adonis! Adonis!”

The sunset dims the light,
and through valleys and woods
they go with red torches,
searching and calling.
Amid tears and laughter,
lament and clamor,
the sorrowing echo
repeats, “Adonis! Adonis!”

The handsomest youth,
the most loving young man,
lies among roses,
cold, pale, and still.
The purple of his veins
stains all the flowers,
and the air is filled
with the cry, “Adonis! Adonis!”

translations.title: The Boat
translations.text:
Laughter and songs!
The clear sun’s rays
pour their smiling brightness
over the waters.
The waves rock a merry boat;
I sit in it with my best friends.

The boat crashes, shattered
into a thousand pieces by the sea.
My friends were poor swimmers;
to their misfortune,
they broke against the rocks of their homeland.
The storm carried me
to the banks of the Seine.

Once more I cross the seas
in a new vessel;
new friends I see
circling around me.
The melancholy voice
of strange seas rocks me.
How far away my homeland is!
How sad my heart!

New song, new laughter!
The wind whistles hard;
the timbers groan, wounded,
beaten by the raging sea.
The last star in the sky
has lost its light.
How sad my breast is!
How far my homeland is!

translations.title: On the Shore of the Deserted Sea
translations.text:
On the shore of the deserted sea,
beside the restless deep,
a young man, full of doubts,
stops in thought,
and thus speaks to the troubled waves:

“Explain to me life’s unknown secret,
the riddle whose discovery
has set so many brows aflame;
heads adorned with pontifical ornaments,
foreheads with solemn miters,
with Damascene turbans,
doctoral caps,
wigs and false hair,
and so many other heads
have sought to know the hidden riddle.
Tell me, I beg you:
What is man? Whence does he come?
Where does his road lead?
What dwells in the high heavens
beyond the burning stars?”

The sea murmurs its eternal song,
sad and drowsy;
the wind blows, the clouds flee;
stars in the void
shine indifferent with their cold radiance,
while a madman waits anxiously for an answer.

translations.title: King Haraldo
translations.text:
In the arms of a lovely fairy
lies noble King Haraldo;
he lies at the bottom of the sea,
and the days pass by.

He can neither live nor die,
so deeply has the fairy bewitched him;
in this sweet torment
he has spent two hundred years.

The king rests his head
upon her alluring lap,
and gazes at her lovely eyes,
never quite done looking.

His hair is silver now,
his body sick and frail;
yellow cheekbones
protrude from his gaunt face.

At times vague tremors
trouble his dreams,
when the storm beats
upon his crystal palace.

At times, far above,
he hears Norman war cries
and suddenly raises his arms,
only to lower them again.

At times he sees sailors in the distance,
singing as they sail;
what the sailors sing
are the glories of King Haraldo.

Then he groans deeply,
and the enchantress, noticing,
bends and smiling presses
a fiery kiss upon his lips.
